brute_force_code:
def flood_fill(grid, sr, sc, color):
    grid = [row[:] for row in grid]
    rows, cols = len(grid), len(grid[0])
    start = grid[sr][sc]
    if start == color:
        return grid
    stack = [(sr, sc)]
    while stack:
        r, c = stack.pop()
        if r < 0 or c < 0 or r >= rows or c >= cols or grid[r][c] != start:
            continue
        grid[r][c] = color
        stack.extend([(r + 1, c), (r - 1, c), (r, c + 1), (r, c - 1)])
    return grid

reference_solution:
def flood_fill(grid, sr, sc, color):
    grid = [row[:] for row in grid]
    rows, cols = len(grid), len(grid[0])
    start = grid[sr][sc]
    if start == color:
        return grid
    visited = set()
    def dfs(r, c):
        if r < 0 or c < 0 or r >= rows or c >= cols:
            return
        if (r, c) in visited or grid[r][c] != start:
            return
        visited.add((r, c))
        grid[r][c] = color
        dfs(r + 1, c)
        dfs(r - 1, c)
        dfs(r, c + 1)
        dfs(r, c - 1)
    dfs(sr, sc)
    return grid

viva.question: What is the time cost of flooding a connected same-color region?
expected_points: each cell enters the flood at most once
worst-case work covers the whole grid
DFS or BFS both stay linear in the flooded region size
neighbor checks are constant work per cell

viva.question: What breaks if the starting cell already has the new color and you still recurse?
expected_points: continuing can loop forever on the same color
returning the grid unchanged is correct
the early exit preserves the original image

viva.question: Why only recolor four-neighbors that still show the original color?
expected_points: connectivity is four-directional in this problem
a different color blocks the flood at that boundary
the invariant is that the flooded set equals the original-color component of the start
